text:
A: Hi there. Gareth. Can you hear me alright?
B: Yes. I'm Abena. Hello.
A: Hello. Where are you?
B: Thornton Heath, in Croydon. You?
A: Maidstone. Kent.
B: I put on my form that your office looked organised. The files with the project numbers.
A: [laughs] That's very generous. Those labels were done by a graduate. If you looked inside, you'd be less impressed.
B: Then I'm glad I didn't look inside.
A: Probably wise. What do you do?
B: Practice administrator at a GP surgery. Part-time. And you, the files are what?
A: Civil engineer. Drainage and flood risk. So if a developer wants to build somewhere that floods, or a culvert collapses under a road, I'm the one who goes and has a look and works out what to do about it.
B: What is a culvert?
A: Sorry, yeah. It's basically a pipe or a tunnel carrying a stream under a road or a railway. When it blocks or falls in, the water's got nowhere to go, so it comes up over the road instead.
B: Like Brigstock Road when it rains.
A: Probably exactly like that, yeah.
B: Is it a stressful job?
A: Er, it can be, for other people. Clients panic. I sort of don't. I'm not sure if that's a skill or I just don't worry enough.
B: Both can be true.
A: [laughs] That's what my partner says. She's a deputy head, Claire. She says I'm hard to read.
B: You are a bit.
A: Fair enough.
B: I'm not complaining. In my work the calm ones are useful. At eight o'clock the phones go mad, everybody wants an appointment, and the receptionist who panics makes it worse for everybody.
A: I can imagine. What's the worst bit for you?
B: People who don't do what they said they would do. Colleagues, I mean. Not patients.
A: Ah. I should probably confess, I'm a bit last-minute with my timesheets.
B: How last-minute?
A: Er... Friday afternoon. Sometimes Monday.
B: Monday is not acceptable.
A: [laughs] No. I know.
B: Somebody is waiting on those numbers, you know. Payroll, billing. They're not doing it for fun.
A: That's fair. I'll do it on time this week. Maybe.
B: Do it Thursday. Then Friday is free.
A: That's actually not a bad system. Do you have children?
B: A son, Kofi. Twenty. At university in Leicester. He comes home in the holidays with a bag of washing.
A: Ha. Mine's nine, Alfie. I'm already dreading that bit. Although I'd quite like the house to myself.
B: It's very quiet. Kwame falls asleep in front of the news every night, and that's the evening.
A: That sounds alright to me, honestly.
B: It's alright. I didn't say it wasn't.
A: [laughs] No. What do you do with the quiet, then?
B: Choir. Church on Sunday. And my tomatoes, they're doing very well this year.
A: I've got a long garden I keep meaning to sort. Mostly nettles at the minute, and a shed that's—
